summary: Defines angular displacement (theta = S/r), its SI unit the radian, conversions between radians/degrees/revolutions, its dimensionless nature, and the conditions under which it behaves as a vector.
title: Angular Displacement

summary: Defines angular velocity as the rate of change of angular displacement, its vector nature and direction via the right-hand rule, its units and dimensions, its relation to tangential velocity (v=r*omega), and its relation to frequency and period (omega=2*pi*f=2*pi/T).
title: Angular Velocity

summary: Defines angular acceleration as the rate of change of angular velocity, its SI unit and dimensions, its vector direction relative to angular velocity, and its relation to tangential linear acceleration (at = r*alpha).
title: 4.4 Angular Acceleration

topicTitle: 4.4 Relation Between Linear and Angular Quantities
summary: Derives the three relations connecting linear and angular quantities for a point on a rotating body: S = R*theta, v = R*omega, and a_t = R*alpha, with worked numeric examples.
title: 4.5 Relation Between Linear and Angular Quantities

summary: Explains why circular motion requires centripetal acceleration and force even at constant speed, derives a_c = v^2/r = r*omega^2, and shows centripetal force F_c = mv^2/r = mr*omega^2 is the net result of real forces like tension, gravity, friction, or the normal force.
title: Centripetal Force and Acceleration

summary: Defines circular motion, distinguishes uniform from non-uniform circular motion, and surveys the key parameters that describe it: angular displacement, angular velocity, angular acceleration, tangential velocity, centripetal acceleration and force, and the fictitious centrifugal force.
title: Circular Motion

summary: Introduces moment of inertia as the rotational analogue of mass, its formula for a point mass and rigid bodies, radius of gyration, torque as the rotational analogue of force, and the rotational form of Newton's Second Law (tau = I*alpha).
title: Torque and Moment of Inertia

summary: Defines angular momentum both as L = r x p (cross product) and L = I*omega for a rigid body, its direction, units, and the law of conservation of angular momentum with the torque-angular-momentum relation.
title: Angular Momentum

topicTitle: 4.9 The Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum
summary: States the Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum (L is constant when net external torque is zero), derives it from tau_net = dL/dt, shows its implication I*omega = constant, applies it to skaters, divers, and star formation, compares it to linear momentum conservation, and explains why internal forces cannot change total angular momentum.
title: The Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum

summary: Defines rotational kinetic energy K.E._rot = (1/2)*I*omega^2, derives it by summing the kinetic energy of every particle in a rigid body, and applies it to rolling objects on an incline, showing a solid disc reaches the bottom faster than a hoop of the same mass and radius because the hoop has a larger moment of inertia.
title: Rotational Kinetic Energy

summary: Explains why banked roads use a component of the normal force to supply centripetal force, derives the ideal banking angle tan(theta) = v^2/(rg) by resolving the normal force, and shows the result is independent of vehicle mass.
title: 4.7 Banking of Roads

summary: Distinguishes natural from artificial satellites, derives orbital velocity v = sqrt(GM/r), surveys satellite types (communication, navigation, Earth observation, scientific) and their orbits, and explains weightlessness in orbit and artificial gravity as consequences of free fall and rotation.
title: Artificial Satellites

summary: Defines the three conditions for a geostationary orbit (24-hour period, equatorial plane, west-to-east direction), derives the orbital radius from F_g = F_c, calculates the altitude (~35,800 km) and orbital velocity (~3.07 km/s), and notes the tradeoffs of latency and launch cost.
title: 4.17 Geostationary Orbits

summary: Derives orbital velocity v = sqrt(GM/r) by setting gravitational force equal to centripetal force, shows it is independent of the orbiting object's mass and decreases with orbital radius, and explains weightlessness in orbit as continuous free fall rather than an absence of gravity.
title: Orbital Velocity

topicTitle: 4.15 Communication Satellites and Weightlessness in Orbit
summary: Covers geostationary communication satellites (orbit at ~35,786 km, 24-hour period, 3 satellites for global coverage, microwave uplink/downlink via transponders, solar power, INTELSAT) and explains why orbiting objects are weightless: the satellite is in continuous free fall, so there is no normal force between an object and its support even though gravity is still acting.
title: Communication Satellites and Weightlessness in Orbit

summary: Distinguishes mass from weight, explains apparent weight as the contact force felt during free fall (falling elevator and orbiting spacecraft), derives orbital (critical) velocity v = sqrt(g(R+h)), and shows how rotating a spacecraft produces artificial gravity via a_c = omega^2*R = g.
title: Weightlessness in Orbit

summary: Explains how rotating a spacecraft creates artificial gravity via centripetal force, derives the required angular velocity omega = sqrt(g/r) and frequency f = (1/2*pi)*sqrt(g/r), and covers practical design challenges: the size-vs-rotation-speed tradeoff, the Coriolis effect, and the gravity gradient.
title: 4.16 Artificial Gravity

summary: Distinguishes real weight (mg) from apparent weight (the normal force a scale reads), and derives the scale reading N in four elevator scenarios: at rest or constant velocity (N=mg), accelerating upward (N=m(g+a)), accelerating downward (N=m(g-a)), and free fall (N=0, weightlessness).
title: Apparent Weight in an Elevator

topicTitle: 4.19 Newton's vs. Einstein's View on Gravitation
summary: Contrasts Newton's view of gravity as an instantaneous force (F = Gm1m2/r^2) with Einstein's General Relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime, covers the experimental evidence for Einstein's theory (starlight bending, Mercury's precession, the Equivalence Principle), and explains orbital weightlessness from both perspectives.
title: Newton's vs. Einstein's View on Gravitation
